title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: After taking his wife upstairs, Levin went to Dolly's part of the house. Darya Alexandrovna was also having a difficult day. She was walking around the room, talking sharply to a little girl who stood roaring in the corner.

"And you shall stand all day in the corner, and have your dinner all by yourself, and not see a single one of your dolls, and I won't make you a new frock," she was saying, at her wits' end how to punish her.
"Oh, she is a horrible child!" she said, turning to Levin. "Where does she pick up such wicked instincts?"
"Why, what's she done?" Levin asked without much interest, for he had come to ask her advice and was annoyed at having arrived at a bad moment.

"Grisha and she went into the raspberries, and there ... I really can't tell you what she did. It's a great pity Miss Elliot isn't with us anymore. This one watches nothing — she's a machine.... _Figurez-vous que la petite_?..."
And Darya Alexandrovna described Masha's crime.
"That proves nothing — it's not a question of wicked instincts at all, it's pure mischief," Levin assured her.
"But something has upset you? What have you come for?" Dolly asked. "What's going on in there?"
And from the tone of her question Levin felt that it would be easy to tell her what he had come to say.
"I wasn't with them — I've been alone in the garden with Kitty. We've had a quarrel for the second time since ... Stiva arrived."
Dolly looked at him with her shrewd, understanding eyes.
"Come, tell me honestly — was there in that gentleman's manner, not in Kitty's, but his, a tone that might be unpleasant — not unpleasant, but horrible, insulting, to a husband?"

"You mean — how shall I put it.... Stay there, stay in the corner!" she said to Masha, who had detected a faint smile on her mother's face and had started to turn around. "The world's verdict would be that he is behaving the way young men behave. _Il fait la cour à une jeune et jolie femme_, and a husband who is a man of the world should only be flattered by it."
"Yes, yes," Levin said gloomily; "but did you notice it?"
"Not only I — Stiva noticed it too. Right after breakfast he said to me in exactly those words: _Je crois que Veslovsky fait un petit brin de cour à Kitty_."
"Well, that settles it. Now I'm satisfied. I'll send him away," said Levin.

"What are you talking about? Have you lost your mind?" Dolly cried, horrified. "Nonsense, Kostya — just think about it!" she said, laughing. "You can go to Fanny now," she said to Masha. "No — if you really want it, I'll talk to Stiva. He'll take him away. He can say you're expecting visitors. He doesn't belong in the house anyway."
"No, no, I'll do it myself."
"But you'll have a row with him?"

"Not at all. I'll enjoy it," said Levin, his eyes flashing with real pleasure. "Come, forgive her, Dolly — she won't do it again," he said about the little sinner, who hadn't gone to Fanny but was standing uncertainly in front of her mother, waiting and looking up from under her brows to catch her mother's eye.
The mother looked at her. The child burst into sobs and hid her face in her mother's lap, and Dolly laid her thin, gentle hand on the child's head.
"And what is there in common between us and him?" thought Levin, and he went off to find Veslovsky.
As he passed through the corridor he gave orders for the carriage to be made ready for a drive to the station.
"The spring broke yesterday," said the footman.
"The covered trap, then — and quickly. Where's our visitor?"
"The gentleman has gone up to his room."
Levin caught Veslovsky just as the man had unpacked his things from his trunk, laid out some new sheet music, and was putting on his gaiters to go out riding.

Whether there was something out of the ordinary in Levin's face, or because Vassenka himself sensed that _ce petit brin de cour_ he had been making was out of place in this household, he was a little (as much as a young man in society can be) thrown by Levin's coming in.
"You ride in gaiters?"
"Yes, it's much cleaner," said Vassenka, putting his stout leg on a chair, fastening the lower hook, smiling with simple-hearted good humor.
He was clearly a good-natured fellow, and Levin, his host, felt sorry for him and ashamed of himself when he saw the shy look on Vassenka's face.

On the table lay a piece of stick that they had broken together that morning testing their strength against each other. Levin picked up the fragment and started smashing it up, snapping bits off the stick, not knowing how to begin.
"I wanted...." He stopped, but then suddenly, remembering Kitty and everything that had happened, he said, looking him squarely in the face: "I've given orders for the horses to be put-to for you."
"What for?" Vassenka began in surprise. "To drive where?"
"For you to drive to the station," Levin said grimly.
"Are you leaving — or has something happened?"

"It happens I'm expecting visitors," said Levin, his strong fingers snapping off the split ends of the stick faster and faster. "And I'm not expecting visitors, and nothing has happened, but I'm asking you to leave. Take my rudeness whatever way you like."
Vassenka drew himself up.
"I'd like an explanation...." he said with dignity, finally getting it.
"I can't explain it," Levin said quietly and deliberately, trying to keep his jaw from trembling; "and you'd be better off not asking."
And when the split ends were all gone, Levin gripped the thick ends in his fingers, snapped the stick in two, and carefully caught the falling piece.

Probably it was the sight of those tense fingers, of the muscles he had seen in action at gymnastics that morning, of the glittering eyes, the soft voice, and the trembling jaw that convinced Vassenka better than any words could. He bowed, shrugged, and smiled scornfully.
"Could I not see Oblonsky?"
The shrug and the smile did not irritate Levin.
"What else was there for him to do?" he thought.
"I'll send him to you right away."

"What sort of madness is this?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said when, after hearing from his friend that he was being thrown out of the house, he found Levin in the garden, where he was walking around waiting for his guest to leave. "_Mais c'est ridicule!_ What fly has stung you? _Mais c'est du dernier ridicule!_ What were you thinking — that just because a young man...."
But the spot where Levin had been stung was clearly still raw — he went pale again as Stepan Arkadyevitch tried to expand on the matter, and he cut him off himself.

"Please don't go into it! I can't help it. I'm ashamed of how I'm treating you and him. But I don't suppose his leaving will be any great sorrow to him, and his presence had become distasteful to me and to my wife."
"But it's an insult to him! _Et puis c'est ridicule_."
"It's both an insult and distressing to me too! And I'm not at fault in any way, and there's no reason I should suffer."
"Well, I really didn't expect this from you! _On peut être jaloux, mais à ce point, c'est du dernier ridicule!_"

Levin turned sharply, walked away from him into the depths of the avenue, and went on pacing up and down alone. Soon he heard the rumble of the trap, and through the trees he saw Vassenka, sitting in the hay (unluckily there had been no seat in the trap), in his Scotch cap, being driven down the avenue, jolting over the ruts.

"What's this?" Levin thought, when a footman ran out of the house and stopped the trap. It was the mechanic — Levin had completely forgotten him. The mechanic, bowing low, said something to Veslovsky, then climbed into the trap, and they drove off together.

Stepan Arkadyevitch and the princess were thoroughly upset by what Levin had done. And Levin himself felt not only thoroughly _ridicule_ but utterly in the wrong and disgraced. But when he remembered what he and his wife had been through, and asked himself how he would behave another time, he answered that he would do exactly the same thing again.

Despite all of this, by the end of that day everyone except the princess — who couldn't forgive Levin's behavior — became extraordinarily lively and good-humored, like children after a scolding or grown-ups after a long, formal reception, so that by evening Vassenka's dismissal was talked about, out of the princess's hearing, as if it had been some remote event. And Dolly, who had inherited her father's gift for telling a funny story, made Varenka helpless with laughter as she told for the third and fourth time, always with fresh comic touches, how she had only just put on her new shoes for the visitor's benefit, and on going into the drawing room had suddenly heard the rumble of the trap. And who should be in it but Vassenka himself, with his Scotch cap, his songs and his gaiters, sitting in the hay.

"If only you'd had the carriage brought out! But no — and then I heard: 'Stop!' Oh, I thought, they've relented. I look out, and behold — a fat German being seated beside him, and off they go.... And my new shoes wasted!..."
